thread.title_full: Ex-Florence County teacher fired over controversial 'Border Patrol' T-shirt photo suing district - NewsBreak

author: Adam Benson
title: Ex-Florence County teacher fired over controversial 'Border Patrol' T-shirt photo suing district - NewsBreak
text:
By Adam Benson ,
1 hours ago
FLORENCE COUNTY, S.C. (WBTW — A former Royall Elementary teaching assistant fired in the wake of a July 2024 cultural celebration event that saw some participants wear “Border Patrol” T-shirts is suing the school district.
Sandra Poston filed a defamation and discrimination lawsuit against Florence School District One on Monday in U.S. District Court, which offers new details into the incident which drew national attention.
A picture posted to the school’s Facebook page on July 31, 2024 depicted staff members wearing sombreros and other Hispanic attire as part of the event. Two people were captured wearing gray “Border Patrol” T-shirts.
Florence One Schools could not immediately be reached for comment, but district officials have said in the past they don’t comment on pending litigation.
In the days that followed, Superintendent Richard O’Malley said several members of the school were placed on administrative leave or terminated — including longtime principal Julie Smith and her assistant, Marci Gatewood.
The images drew the ire of groups including Racial Justice Network, a national civil rights group, and the Florence County Democratic Party.
Royall Elementary posted an apology of its own on Facebook a day after the photo surfaced.
“At Royall, we take great pride in our long-standing tradition of embracing and supporting every student who walks through the doors of our building,” the statement said. “Our staff is unanimously committed to celebrating the diversity of our families and enduring that each and every student at Royall is successful, happy and recognized for his or her unique culture and abilities.”
O’Malley’s decision to fire the school’s administrators and others involved was unpopular among Royall Elementary teachers.
““There’s not a single staff member who has a clear mind and heart. The loss of the five individuals from our Royall Elementary family cuts deep,” Royall Elementary third grade teacher Alissa Bennett said during an Aug. 21, 2024 Florence 1 Schools board meeting. “You have let us down. You have let an entire community down.”
In her complaint, Poston — who had worked in the school for 20 years — said Smith and Gatewood organized the “compulsory” event, appointing teams to represent nations competing in the Olympics.
“Each team was to have a table with clothing, decorations and food representative of their country’s culture and traditions,” the lawsuit said.
Poston’s team included six other people who were given Mexico as their country.
“For the activity … (a) team member proposed the idea of a game of ‘red light/green light,’ with the border between Mexico and the United States as the finish line. On a signal, participants ran from a fixed point to the ‘border,’ where the winner was awarded a prize,” according to the lawsuit. “The activity was approved and adopted by the entire team. The team decided to have ‘U.S. Border Patrol’ agents at the finish line.”
Poston, who was one the people caught on camera wearing a T-shirt, said she purchased blank ones that were printed with the phrase. Smith and Gatewood were aware ahead of time about the idea, her complaint says.
Royall Elementary lawsuit Download Royall Elementary’s Facebook page posted a collection of photos from the event, sparking controversy. By Aug. 1, Poston and two others including a Black man who worked as a janitor, her suit says. Smith and Gatewood were also forced to resign.
Poston appealed to O’Malley, who denied it on “the false grounds that (Poston) had not been truthful during the course of the investigation,” her complaint says.
Later, district officials reinstated the Black man. Poston went on to file a sex discrimination complaint with the South Carolina Human Affairs Commission, which then referred it to the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.
The case was eventually dismissed.
Poston also said O’Malley went out of his way to tarnish her reputation by singling her and two other team members out as the “perpetuators of a hateful, racist, activity,” her lawsuit claims. “The defamatory statements have caused injury to (Poston’s) standing among her peers, and have damaged her social relationships such that she has been shunned by others who were formerly warm and involved in her life.”
